- When sentiment is consistently negative (last 3–5 days), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to account for mean reversion; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope after peak.
- If sentiment is positive and price is trending upward, model frequently overestimates momentum; cap upward forecasts at 1.5x recent 7-day average or add a 1–2 day lagged decay factor.
- In multi-day forecast horizons (e.g., 30d), model often underestimates late-period volatility; increase final 5–7 days’ forecast by 2–5% to reflect sentiment-driven momentum.
- When sentiment history shows repeated small negative swings, model tends to ignore them; add a 0.5–1.0% upward bias to counteract downward bias in early forecast days.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often defaults to historical mean; use sentiment-weighted moving average (e.g., 30d sentiment avg) to adjust baseline forecast.
